chapters.title: Sensory Pathways and the Somatic Nervous System
The Autonomic Nervous System and Higher-Order Functions

topics.title: Brain regions and surface landmarks
topics.cue: Cerebrum: conscious work. Cerebellum: coordinate. Brainstem: the connection.

notes.text: The book groups the adult brain into cerebrum, cerebellum, diencephalon, and brainstem.
Midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata form the brainstem; the medulla links it with the spinal cord.
Conscious thought, intellectual functions, memory, and regulation of skeletal-muscle activity.
Coordinates complex motor patterns and adjusts ongoing movement.
Gyri are raised folds; sulci are shallower grooves; fissures are deeper grooves. Cortex is a superficial gray-matter layer.

questions.prompt: Which set contains only the three brainstem regions?
questions.explanation: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.

questions.prompt: Which major region is most associated with conscious thought and intellectual functions in the course overview?
questions.explanation: The overview associates the cerebrum with conscious thought, intellect, and memory.

questions.prompt: What is the name for an elevated fold on the cerebral surface?
questions.explanation: A gyrus is a raised fold; sulci and fissures are grooves.

questions.prompt: Which region helps adjust ongoing movements rather than serving as the principal site of conscious thought?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates motor patterns and adjusts motor output.

topics.title: Brain vesicles and adult derivatives
topics.cue: Forebrain splits in two; hindbrain splits in two; midbrain keeps its name.

notes.text: Prosencephalon (forebrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and rhombencephalon (hindbrain).
Telencephalon becomes the cerebrum with lateral ventricles; diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle.
Mesencephalon remains the midbrain; its cavity becomes the cerebral aqueduct.
Metencephalon produces pons and cerebellum; myelencephalon produces medulla oblongata. Both relate to the fourth ventricle.

questions.prompt: Which secondary vesicle develops into the cerebrum?
questions.explanation: The development table pairs telencephalon with cerebrum and lateral ventricles.

questions.prompt: Which secondary vesicle produces both the pons and cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The metencephalon is a hindbrain subdivision that forms the pons and cerebellum.

questions.prompt: Which adult structure develops from the myelencephalon?
questions.explanation: The myelencephalon develops into the medulla oblongata.

questions.prompt: Which primary vesicle does not split into two secondary vesicles in the course table?
questions.explanation: The mesencephalon remains the midbrain; forebrain and hindbrain subdivide.

topics.title: Ventricles and connecting passages
topics.cue: Lateral → foramen → third → aqueduct → fourth.

notes.text: One lies in each cerebral hemisphere; the septum pellucidum separates them.
Lies within the diencephalon; each lateral ventricle communicates with it through an interventricular foramen.
Narrow midbrain passage connecting the third and fourth ventricles.
Related to the pons, upper medulla, and cerebellum; continuous inferiorly with the spinal cord central canal.
Ependymal cells line the ventricles. Distinguish a fluid-filled chamber from the tissue surrounding it.

questions.prompt: Which passage connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle?
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain between the third and fourth ventricles.

questions.prompt: Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle through which opening?
questions.explanation: The interventricular foramina connect the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.

questions.prompt: Which cells line the ventricles?
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells form the ventricular lining described in the textbook.

questions.prompt: Which ventricle lies in the diencephalon?
questions.explanation: The third ventricle is the ventricular chamber of the diencephalon.

topics.title: CSF production, circulation, and balance
topics.cue: Produce → circulate → cushion → return to venous blood.

notes.text: Choroid plexuses produce and maintain cerebrospinal fluid; the textbook describes specialized ependymal cells controlling its composition.
CSF supports the brain by buoyancy, cushions neural tissue, and transports nutrients, chemical signals, and wastes.
From the fourth ventricle, CSF enters the subarachnoid space through two lateral apertures and one median aperture; arachnoid granulations return it to venous circulation.
The course gives approximately 150 mL present at a time and replacement about every eight hours. Production and absorption normally balance.
Accumulation can occur when circulation or resorption is impaired. The lecture distinguishes it from cerebral edema, or tissue swelling.
The lecture's plasma-minus-clotting-factors shorthand differs from the textbook's description of selectively produced CSF. See Source notes; no question relies on treating them as identical.

questions.prompt: Where is CSF produced and maintained?
questions.explanation: Choroid plexuses produce CSF; venous sinuses receive returning fluid rather than producing it.

questions.prompt: Which structure returns CSF to the venous circulation?
questions.explanation: Arachnoid granulations project toward dural venous sinuses and allow CSF resorption.

questions.prompt: From the fourth ventricle, which openings lead to the subarachnoid space?
options: Two lateral apertures and one median aperture
Two optic canals and one jugular foramen
The central sulcus and lateral sulcus
questions.explanation: These apertures connect the fourth ventricle with the subarachnoid space.

questions.prompt: Which is a listed function of CSF?
questions.explanation: CSF provides buoyancy, cushioning, and a transport medium.

questions.prompt: What can impaired CSF resorption cause?
options: Formation of a new cranial nerve
questions.explanation: Failure of fluid removal can cause abnormal CSF accumulation.

topics.title: Cranial meninges and dural folds
topics.cue: Dura outside, arachnoid middle, pia hugs the brain.

notes.text: Superficial to deep: dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater. CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.
Has periosteal and meningeal layers; the outer layer attaches to the skull. Dural venous sinuses collect venous blood.
Projects between the cerebral hemispheres within the longitudinal cerebral fissure.
Separates the cerebral hemispheres from the cerebellum.
Projects between the two cerebellar hemispheres.

questions.prompt: Which meninx closely follows the brain surface?
questions.explanation: The pia mater closely adheres to the brain surface; the arachnoid does not follow every fold.

questions.prompt: Which dural fold separates the cerebral hemispheres?
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri extends into the longitudinal cerebral fissure.

questions.prompt: Which fold separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum?
questions.explanation: The tentorium cerebelli forms the partition above the cerebellum.

questions.prompt: CSF in the subarachnoid space lies between which layers?
questions.explanation: The subarachnoid space is between arachnoid mater and pia mater.

topics.title: Blood–brain and blood–CSF barriers
topics.cue: BBB: endothelial junctions. Blood–CSF barrier: specialized ependymal cells.

notes.text: Capillary endothelial cells joined by tight junctions restrict movement into CNS tissue.
Support the barrier by influencing endothelial junctions and permeability; they are not a substitute name for the endothelial layer.
The sources describe lipid-soluble substances and gases crossing more readily, while other substances require selective transport.
The course highlights portions of the hypothalamus, posterior pituitary, pineal gland, and choroid plexuses.
Specialized ependymal cells around choroid plexus capillaries provide a separate selective barrier.

questions.prompt: Which cells form the tightly joined capillary lining central to the BBB?
questions.explanation: Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells are central to the BBB.

questions.prompt: What role do astrocytes have in the BBB according to the sources?
options: They influence endothelial permeability and junctions
They replace all blood vessels with axons
They carry CSF to the kidneys
questions.explanation: Astrocytes provide signals that support and regulate the endothelial barrier.

questions.prompt: Which cells create the blood–CSF barrier at the choroid plexus?
questions.explanation: Specialized ependymal cells joined by tight junctions control access to CSF at the choroid plexus.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the areas highlighted as an exception to the usual BBB pattern?
questions.explanation: The lecture and textbook list the pineal gland among the highlighted exceptions.

topics.title: Medulla: vital centers and relays
topics.cue: Medulla: basic rhythm, cardiovascular control, and sensory relay.

notes.text: The medulla is the most inferior brainstem region and connects with the spinal cord.
Cardiovascular centers include cardiac and vasomotor components. Respiratory rhythmicity centers establish the basic respiratory pace.
Gracile and cuneate nuclei relay somatic sensory information toward the thalamus.
The course associates the medulla with cranial nerves VIII in part, IX, X, XI in part, and XII, and with the reticular formation.
Relays motor-related information to the cerebellum.

questions.prompt: Which region contains the respiratory rhythmicity centers described as setting the basic breathing pace?
questions.explanation: The course locates the basic respiratory rhythmicity centers in the medulla.

questions.prompt: The cardiac and vasomotor centers are subdivisions of which group?
questions.explanation: The lecture subdivides cardiovascular control into cardiac and vasomotor centers.

questions.prompt: Gracile and cuneate nuclei relay somatic sensory information toward which structure?
questions.explanation: These medullary nuclei relay ascending somatic sensory information toward the thalamus.

questions.prompt: Which brainstem region directly connects with the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The medulla is the inferior connection between the brain and spinal cord.

topics.title: Pons and reading tract names
topics.cue: A tract name is a travel direction: origin first, destination second.

notes.text: The pons contains relay nuclei and tracts linking the cerebellum with other CNS regions.
Apneustic and pneumotaxic centers modify medullary respiratory activity in this course's terminology.
The course lists V, VI, VII, and VIII in part with the pons.
Spinothalamic travels from spinal cord toward thalamus; corticospinal travels from cerebral cortex toward spinal cord.

questions.prompt: In the course naming rule, what does the first part of a tract name usually indicate?
questions.explanation: The lecture teaches origin first and destination second when interpreting these tract names.

questions.prompt: A spinothalamic tract carries information from where to where?
questions.explanation: Spino- identifies spinal origin; -thalamic identifies the thalamic destination.

questions.prompt: Which pontine centers modify medullary respiratory activity in the course?
questions.explanation: These pontine centers adjust the respiratory rhythmicity centers of the medulla.

questions.prompt: Which cranial-nerve group is associated with the pons in the lecture?
options: V, VI, VII, and VIII in part
questions.explanation: The pons slide identifies nuclei for V, VI, VII, and VIII in part.

topics.title: Midbrain: colliculi, nuclei, and peduncles
topics.cue: Superior colliculi: sight. Inferior colliculi: sound.

notes.text: Roof of the midbrain, posterior to the cerebral aqueduct; includes superior and inferior colliculi (corpora quadrigemina).
Superior colliculi organize visual reflex responses; inferior colliculi process auditory information and auditory reflex responses.
Includes the red nucleus and substantia nigra in the course description.
Participates in subconscious upper-limb position and muscle-tone control.
Dopamine-producing region involved in basal-nuclei regulation.
Fiber bundles connecting cerebral regions with lower CNS structures; distinguish cerebral from cerebellar peduncles.

questions.prompt: A sudden bright light triggers reflexive head and eye movements. Which midbrain structures are highlighted for this role?
questions.explanation: The superior colliculi are associated with reflex responses to visual stimuli.

questions.prompt: Which midbrain structures are associated with auditory reflex processing?
questions.explanation: The inferior colliculi process auditory information and reflex responses.

questions.prompt: Which neurotransmitter is associated with neurons of the substantia nigra in this chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter links substantia nigra neurons with dopamine and regulation of basal-nuclei activity.

questions.prompt: Which nucleus is associated with subconscious upper-limb position and background muscle tone?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is identified with upper-limb position and muscle-tone regulation.

questions.prompt: The superior and inferior colliculi together are called what?
questions.explanation: The two pairs of colliculi are collectively the corpora quadrigemina.

topics.title: Cerebellar structure and coordination
topics.cue: Arbor vitae = white tree; Purkinje cells = cortical processing.

notes.text: Folia are surface folds; the vermis is a narrow midline cortical band; the primary fissure separates anterior and posterior lobes.
Cerebellar cortex and nuclei are gray matter. Arbor vitae is the branching internal white matter.
Large, highly branched neurons in the cerebellar cortex receive extensive input.
Superior links with midbrain and higher centers; middle communicates with pons; inferior links with medulla and spinal cord.
Compares sensory feedback with motor activity to maintain posture, balance, and smooth movement. Ataxia means impaired coordination.

questions.prompt: What is the arbor vitae?
options: Branching white matter of the cerebellum
questions.explanation: Its tree-like appearance in section gives cerebellar white matter the name arbor vitae.

questions.prompt: Which cells are large, highly branched neurons of the cerebellar cortex?
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are prominent processing neurons in cerebellar cortical tissue.

questions.prompt: Which cerebellar peduncles communicate primarily with the pons?
questions.explanation: Middle cerebellar peduncles carry communications with the pons.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the impaired coordination discussed with cerebellar damage?
questions.explanation: The lecture uses ataxia for deterioration of muscular coordination.

questions.prompt: Which midline cerebellar landmark is named in the source figures?
questions.explanation: The vermis lies along the cerebellar midline.

topics.title: Thalamic relay and geniculate bodies
topics.cue: Lateral geniculate = visual; medial geniculate = auditory.

notes.text: The thalamus relays and processes sensory information bound for the cerebral cortex; the book identifies olfactory input as an exception to the usual initial relay.
Receives visual information and projects toward visual cortex.
Relays auditory information toward auditory cortex.
Ventral nuclei participate in somatic sensory and motor relays; anterior nuclei are part of the limbic system. These details are expanded in the textbook.

questions.prompt: Which thalamic structure relays visual information toward the visual cortex?
questions.explanation: The lateral geniculate body is the visual relay highlighted in the thalamus figure.

questions.prompt: Which thalamic structure relays auditory information?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body is associated with auditory input and output.

questions.prompt: Which major sensory route is the textbook's exception to the usual thalamic relay before reaching cerebral areas?
questions.explanation: The textbook singles out the olfactory tract when describing the usual ascending thalamic relay.

topics.title: Diencephalon and hypothalamic control
topics.cue: Hypothalamus: homeostasis; epithalamus: pineal gland.

notes.text: Includes epithalamus, thalamus, and hypothalamus. The pineal gland of the epithalamus secretes melatonin.
Forms the diencephalic floor and links nervous-system activity with endocrine and autonomic regulation.
Connects the hypothalamus with the pituitary gland.
Supra-optic produces ADH; paraventricular produces oxytocin; pre-optic regulates temperature; suprachiasmatic regulates daily rhythms in the course table.
Hypothalamic centers participate in hunger, thirst, satiety, and emotional/autonomic responses.

questions.prompt: Which stalk connects the hypothalamus with the pituitary gland?
questions.explanation: The infundibulum is the hypothalamic–pituitary stalk.

questions.prompt: Which nucleus is paired with daily circadian rhythms in the supplied table?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamic table identifies the suprachiasmatic nucleus with daily rhythms.

questions.prompt: Which hypothalamic region is paired with regulation of body temperature?
questions.explanation: The pre-optic area coordinates thermoregulatory responses in the course description.

questions.prompt: Which hormone is produced by the supra-optic nucleus in the supplied table?
questions.explanation: The table pairs the supra-optic nucleus with ADH and the paraventricular nucleus with oxytocin.

topics.title: Limbic system, hippocampus, and amygdala
topics.cue: Hippocampus: new memories. Amygdala: emotional associations. Fornix: connecting tract.

notes.text: The limbic system is described as a functional rather than a single anatomical division; it links emotion, motivation, and memory.
Important for learning and new long-term memory storage/retrieval in the textbook framing.
Links emotions with memories and participates in fear/anxiety-related responses.
White-matter tract connecting the hippocampus with the hypothalamus, including mammillary bodies.
Cingulate, parahippocampal, and dentate gyri belong to the limbic lobe description.

questions.prompt: Which system is described as a functional grouping involved in emotion, motivation, and memory?
questions.explanation: The limbic system groups connected structures by their shared functions.

questions.prompt: Which structure is especially important for forming new long-term memories?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is central to new long-term memory processing in the supplied text.

questions.prompt: What kind of structure is the fornix?
questions.explanation: The fornix is a cerebral white-matter tract connecting limbic structures.

questions.prompt: Which structure is associated with linking emotional states to memories?
questions.explanation: The textbook associates the amygdaloid body with emotional responses and memory associations.

topics.title: Cerebral lobes, white matter, and basal nuclei
topics.cue: Association: same hemisphere. Commissural: across hemispheres. Projection: other CNS levels.

notes.text: Central sulcus separates frontal and parietal lobes. Lateral sulcus relates to the temporal lobe; the insula is deep to it.
Association fibers connect cortical areas within one hemisphere; commissural fibers connect hemispheres; projection fibers connect cortex with other CNS levels.
A major commissural fiber bundle between hemispheres.
Include caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus; involved in subconscious adjustment of movement patterns and muscle tone.
Contains lateral putamen and medial globus pallidus in the textbook description.

questions.prompt: The central sulcus separates which lobes?
questions.explanation: The precentral frontal gyrus and postcentral parietal gyrus border the central sulcus.

questions.prompt: Which fibers connect cortical areas within the same hemisphere?
questions.explanation: Association fibers remain within one cerebral hemisphere.

questions.prompt: The corpus callosum is an example of which fiber class?
questions.explanation: Commissural fibers permit communication between cerebral hemispheres.

questions.prompt: Which component of the lentiform nucleus is more medial?
questions.explanation: The textbook places globus pallidus medial to the putamen.

topics.title: Motor, sensory, association, and language areas
topics.cue: Precentral moves; postcentral feels. Association areas interpret and organize.

notes.text: On the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe; directs voluntary skeletal-muscle commands.
On the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe; receives general somatic sensory information.
Visual cortex is occipital; auditory and olfactory cortex are temporal in the course map; gustatory cortex is shown at the insula/adjacent frontal area.
Interpret sensory input or coordinate learned movement patterns; premotor cortex stores learned motor patterns in this account.

Broca's area is associated with speech production; Wernicke's with comprehension, generally emphasized in the left hemisphere. The text notes individual variation and participation of both hemispheres.
Integrates information for intellectual functions such as predicting consequences.

questions.prompt: Where is the primary motor cortex located?
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus is the cortical motor region identified in the source.

questions.prompt: Where is the primary somatosensory cortex located?
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus receives general somatic sensory input.

questions.prompt: Which area is most directly associated with speech production in the course?
questions.explanation: Broca's area coordinates patterns needed for speech production.

questions.prompt: Which area is most directly associated with language comprehension in the course?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is associated with language comprehension in the source description.

questions.prompt: Which lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
questions.explanation: The primary visual cortex is mapped to the occipital lobe.

topics.title: Twelve cranial nerves: principal functions
topics.cue: Names and functions first; then compare nearby nerves that are easy to confuse.

notes.text: Olfactory = smell; optic = vision.
Oculomotor controls most extrinsic eye muscles and levator palpebrae; trochlear supplies superior oblique; abducens supplies lateral rectus.
Trigeminal supplies facial sensation and muscles of mastication; facial controls facial expression and carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Vestibulocochlear carries hearing and balance; glossopharyngeal includes posterior one-third tongue taste, pharyngeal functions, and carotid sensory input.
Vagus is widely distributed to thoracic/abdominal viscera; accessory supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius through its external branch; hypoglossal controls tongue movement.
This complete nerve review comes from the textbook. The uploaded Chapter 14 lecture files do not contain a full dedicated cranial-nerve review.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve is responsible for smell?
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerves carry the special sensation of smell.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle?
questions.explanation: The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique; abducens supplies lateral rectus.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle?
questions.explanation: Abducens activates lateral rectus, associated with abduction of the eye.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve is paired with muscles of mastication?
questions.explanation: The mandibular division of trigeminal carries motor fibers to muscles of mastication.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve controls facial-expression muscles and carries anterior two-thirds taste?
questions.explanation: Facial has these motor and sensory functions; glossopharyngeal carries posterior one-third taste.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries hearing and equilibrium information?
questions.explanation: Its cochlear branch carries hearing and its vestibular branch carries balance information.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve controls tongue movements?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve provides motor supply to the tongue.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve is widely distributed through thoracic and abdominal viscera?
questions.explanation: The vagus is the widely distributed cranial nerve described in the textbook.

topics.title: Cranial divisions, passages, and reflex links
topics.cue: V has three divisions; III, VII, IX, X carry parasympathetic outflow.

notes.text: Ophthalmic V1 and maxillary V2 are sensory; mandibular V3 is mixed.
V1 uses superior orbital fissure; V2 foramen rotundum; V3 foramen ovale. Optic nerve uses optic canal; hypoglossal uses hypoglossal canal.
Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X carry these autonomic fibers.
Contact with the cornea uses trigeminal afferents and facial efferents to blink.
Vestibulocochlear input helps coordinate III, IV, and VI motor output to stabilize vision with head movement.
The book's cranial-reflex and visceral-reflex tables conflict in their wording of a pupillary light response. This initial bank does not test that disputed row.

questions.prompt: Which trigeminal division carries both sensory and motor fibers?
questions.explanation: V3 carries sensory fibers and the motor supply to muscles of mastication.

questions.prompt: Which passage does the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve use?
questions.explanation: The source pairs V2 with foramen rotundum and V3 with foramen ovale.

questions.prompt: Which group carries cranial parasympathetic output?
questions.explanation: The source identifies III, VII, IX, and X as the cranial carriers of parasympathetic fibers.

questions.prompt: Which afferent/efferent pair belongs to the corneal blink reflex?
questions.explanation: The cranial-reflex table pairs trigeminal sensory input with facial motor output for blinking.

topics.title: EEG and brain-wave vocabulary
topics.cue: Use the course pairings: alpha resting, beta concentrating, delta deep sleep.

notes.text: An electroencephalogram is a recording of brain electrical activity; the observed patterns are called brain waves.
The supplied text associates alpha waves with awake adults resting with eyes closed.
Associated with attention, concentration, or psychological tension in the source.
Large-amplitude, low-frequency waves associated with deep sleep in the course figure.
These are the textbook's introductory study pairings, not a clinical interpretation guide for an individual's EEG.

questions.prompt: What does an electroencephalogram record?
questions.explanation: An EEG records brain electrical activity as wave patterns.

questions.prompt: Which wave category is associated with awake resting adults with eyes closed in the supplied text?
questions.explanation: The course associates alpha with relaxed awake rest and beta with concentration.

questions.prompt: Which wave category is associated with intense concentration in the course figure?
options: All categories mean the same thing
questions.explanation: Beta is paired with concentration in the supplied figure.

questions.prompt: Which category is associated with deep sleep in the source figure?
questions.explanation: The figure pairs delta waves with deep sleep.

topics.title: Sensation, perception, and sensory coding
topics.cue: Sensation arrives; perception is awareness.

notes.text: Sensory pathways deliver information toward CNS processing centers; somatic motor pathways distribute commands to skeletal muscle.
Sensation is arriving sensory information; perception is conscious awareness of that information.
The textbook describes conversion of a stimulus into receptor electrical activity that can lead to action potentials in a sensory neuron.
A receptor is particularly sensitive to a certain type of stimulus; structure and accessory tissues influence what it detects.
Stimulus intensity is conveyed by firing frequency and pattern, not by making each action potential taller. A labeled line links a modality with its central destination.

questions.prompt: What is perception in the course terminology?
options: Every motor command leaving the CNS
questions.explanation: Perception is the conscious awareness of arriving sensory information.

questions.prompt: A receptor responds strongly to pressure but not to the same amount of chemical stimulation. Which concept is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Receptor specificity describes sensitivity to particular stimulus types.

questions.prompt: How is a stronger sustained sensory stimulus commonly represented along its sensory axon?
options: Increased height of every action potential
Conversion of the axon into a gland
Reversal of every action potential's direction
questions.explanation: The textbook describes frequency and pattern as the sensory code rather than variable action-potential height.

questions.prompt: Which division carries sensory input toward the CNS?
questions.explanation: Afferent pathways convey arriving sensory information.

topics.title: Receptive fields and adaptation
topics.cue: Small field = precise location. Phasic = change; tonic = ongoing.

notes.text: Area monitored by one receptor cell/sensory neuron in the course description. A larger field makes precise localization harder.
Remain active and show little or slow adaptation; their firing rate reflects stimulation.
Respond especially to changing conditions and adapt rapidly to a stable stimulus.
Reduced sensitivity or awareness during continuing stimulation.
Peripheral adaptation changes receptor activity; central adaptation reduces transmission/awareness along CNS pathways even when sensory input continues.

questions.prompt: Which receptive field would generally provide more precise localization?
options: Any field with fewer boundaries is equally precise
questions.explanation: A smaller field narrows the region from which the stimulus could have arisen.

questions.prompt: Which receptor pattern best emphasizes a change in stimulation rather than a continuing stable stimulus?
questions.explanation: Phasic receptors respond particularly to changes and adapt quickly.

questions.prompt: Which receptor category is described as always active in the course?
questions.explanation: Tonic receptors provide ongoing activity that changes with stimulation.

questions.prompt: Reduced transmission along a CNS sensory pathway despite continuing receptor input is which textbook category?
questions.explanation: Central adaptation occurs within CNS processing pathways; peripheral adaptation involves the receptor's activity.

topics.title: General senses and receptor classes
topics.cue: Extero = outside; intero = inside; proprio = position.

notes.text: Exteroceptors monitor the external environment, interoceptors monitor internal organs, and proprioceptors report body position and movement.
Nociceptors respond to damaging/pain-associated stimuli, thermoreceptors to temperature, mechanoreceptors to physical distortion, and chemoreceptors to chemicals.
Free nerve endings with large receptive fields; respond to extremes of temperature, mechanical damage, or chemicals released with injury.
The lecture explicitly says the fast-pain versus slow-pain distinction will not be asked for exam purposes. It is not tested in this bank.

questions.prompt: Which receptor category monitors body position and movement?
questions.explanation: Proprioceptors supply information about skeletal-muscle and joint position or movement.

questions.prompt: Which receptor type is also called a pain receptor?
questions.explanation: Nociceptors detect stimuli associated with potential or actual tissue damage in this course.

questions.prompt: Which receptor class is sensitive to physical distortion of its membrane?
questions.explanation: Mechanoreceptors respond to pressure, stretch, or related mechanical distortion.

questions.prompt: Which category monitors the internal environment of visceral organs?
questions.explanation: Interoceptors monitor internal organs and their conditions.

topics.title: Six tactile receptors in the skin
topics.cue: Hair moves its plexus; lamellar layers detect deep pressure; tactile corpuscles detect fine touch.

notes.text: Branching sensory endings that respond to touch, pressure, pain, and temperature in the supplied figure.
Free nerve endings stimulated by movement of a hair.
Merkel-cell-associated endings for fine touch, pressure, shape, and texture.
Ruffini corpuscles respond to pressure and distortion of the deep dermis.
Pacinian corpuscles respond to deep pressure and high-frequency vibration; concentric lamellae are distinctive in the source image.
Meissner corpuscles detect fine touch, pressure, and low-frequency vibration.

questions.prompt: Which receptor is stimulated by hair movement?
questions.explanation: A root hair plexus consists of sensory endings associated with the hair root.

questions.prompt: Which skin receptors are associated with shape and texture?
questions.explanation: Tactile discs detect fine touch and pressure and are sensitive to shape and texture.

questions.prompt: Which receptor detects deep pressure and high-frequency vibration?
questions.explanation: The supplied figure identifies lamellar corpuscles with deep pressure and high-frequency vibration.

questions.prompt: Which receptor detects fine touch and low-frequency vibration?
questions.explanation: Tactile corpuscles are paired with fine touch, pressure, and low-frequency vibration.

questions.prompt: Bulbous or Ruffini corpuscles are associated with what?
options: Pressure and distortion of the deep dermis
questions.explanation: The figure places bulbous corpuscles in the deep dermis and associates them with distortion and pressure.

topics.title: Baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, and proprioceptors
topics.cue: Baro measures pressure; chemo measures chemical conditions.

notes.text: Detect stretch associated with pressure or volume changes, including arterial sinuses, lungs, digestive tract, and urinary bladder.
The lecture shows medullary receptors monitoring CSF pH/CO2; carotid and aortic bodies monitor blood pH, CO2, and O2.
Carotid-body information is associated with CN IX; aortic-body information with CN X in the source figure.
The textbook distinguishes muscle spindles (muscle length), Golgi tendon organs (tension), and joint-capsule receptors (position/movement).

questions.prompt: Which receptor type in the carotid sinus provides information about blood pressure?
questions.explanation: Baroreceptors detect stretch associated with pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries carotid-body chemoreceptor information in the lecture figure?
questions.explanation: The source figure labels the carotid-body sensory route with CN IX.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries aortic-body chemoreceptor information in that figure?
questions.explanation: The figure pairs aortic-body sensory input with CN X.

questions.prompt: Which proprioceptor is most directly associated with muscle length?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles provide length-related proprioceptive input; Golgi tendon organs monitor tension.

topics.title: Ascending sensory pathways and neuron orders
topics.cue: Spinothalamic: crude/pain/temperature. Posterior column: fine/vibration/position. Spinocerebellar: coordination.

notes.text: First-order sensory neurons deliver input to the CNS. Second-order neurons relay it; for conscious pathways, third-order thalamic neurons project to cortex.
Anterior tracts carry crude touch/pressure; lateral tracts carry pain/temperature. Second-order neurons cross in the spinal cord before ascending.
Carries fine touch, vibration, pressure, and proprioception; relays in medullary gracile/cuneate nuclei, then crosses toward the medial lemniscus.
Delivers proprioceptive information to the cerebellum for subconscious coordination rather than primary conscious perception.
The cortical map reflects relative sensory input, not a scale drawing of the physical size of body parts.

questions.prompt: Which tract is associated with pain and temperature in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensations.

questions.prompt: Which pathway carries highly localized fine touch and vibration toward conscious perception?
questions.explanation: The posterior column pathway carries fine touch, vibration, pressure, and proprioception.

questions.prompt: Where do second-order spinothalamic axons cross in the supplied pathway description?
questions.explanation: They cross within the spinal cord before ascending toward the thalamus.

questions.prompt: The spinocerebellar pathway carries information primarily to which destination?
questions.explanation: It provides the cerebellum with proprioceptive information for movement coordination.

questions.prompt: In the conscious sensory pathways shown, third-order neuron cell bodies are found in which region?
questions.explanation: Third-order thalamic neurons relay to the primary somatosensory cortex.

topics.title: Somatic motor pathways and decussation
topics.cue: Upper motor neuron directs; lower motor neuron reaches the muscle.

notes.text: Upper motor neurons lie in CNS motor centers and influence lower motor neurons. Lower motor axons innervate skeletal muscle.
Carries commands to lower motor neurons in cranial-nerve motor nuclei of the brainstem.
Carries commands to lower motor neurons in spinal anterior horns. Lateral fibers cross at the medullary pyramids; anterior fibers cross near their spinal destination in the course table.
Vestibulospinal supports balance/tone; tectospinal coordinates responses to visual/auditory input; reticulospinal modifies reflex activity.
Rubrospinal originates in red nuclei and contributes to upper-limb motor control.

questions.prompt: Which neuron directly innervates skeletal muscle in the somatic motor pathway?
questions.explanation: Lower motor neuron axons form the final somatic motor connection to skeletal muscle.

questions.prompt: Which tract carries commands to motor nuclei of cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: Corticobulbar fibers descend to brainstem cranial-nerve motor nuclei.

questions.prompt: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross according to the supplied table?
questions.explanation: The lateral corticospinal fibers decussate at the medullary pyramids.

questions.prompt: Which descending tract arises from red nuclei?
questions.explanation: Rubrospinal fibers originate in the red nuclei of the midbrain.

questions.prompt: Which descending pathway is especially associated with balance and muscle tone?
questions.explanation: Vestibulospinal tracts carry postural and balance-related motor commands.

topics.title: Referred pain and motor feedback
topics.cue: Location felt is not always location of origin; movement is continuously adjusted.

notes.text: Visceral pain can be perceived at another location. The lecture specifically cautions that cardiac pain may be felt in the left arm, but not always.
Supply background patterns and adjust upper motor neuron activity rather than directly innervating the skeletal muscle.
Monitors proprioceptive, visual, and vestibular information and adjusts motor commands to improve smoothness and precision.
The textbook describes learned patterns becoming smoother through repeated movement and feedback.

questions.prompt: What does referred pain mean in this chapter?
options: Pain is perceived away from its actual source
Every pain receptor has stopped firing
Motor commands are perceived as light
Pain occurs only in the cerebral cortex
questions.explanation: Referred pain concerns a mismatch between the origin of visceral input and its perceived location.

questions.prompt: Which statement preserves the lecture's caution about cardiac referred pain?
options: It may be felt in the left arm, but not always
It must always be felt only in the left arm
It never involves any region outside the chest
Its location alone proves a diagnosis
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly includes the qualification 'but not always'; it does not make location diagnostic.

questions.prompt: Which structure uses sensory feedback to fine-tune ongoing movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum compares sensory information and motor activity to refine movement.

questions.prompt: Do the basal nuclei directly innervate skeletal muscle fibers in these pathways?
options: No; they adjust motor pathway activity
Yes; their axons replace lower motor neurons
Yes; they form every motor end plate
questions.explanation: The textbook describes basal-nuclei effects through upper motor pathways and feedback loops, not direct muscle innervation.

topics.title: Somatic versus autonomic motor organization
topics.cue: Somatic: CNS neuron → skeletal muscle. Autonomic: pre → ganglion → post → viscera.

notes.text: Somatic output targets skeletal muscle; autonomic output targets smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands, and adipocytes.
Has a cell body in the CNS and an axon that extends to an autonomic ganglion.
Has its cell body in a peripheral autonomic ganglion; its postganglionic axon extends to a visceral target.
The hypothalamus contains integrative autonomic centers; brainstem and spinal centers participate in reflex regulation.
Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often oppose one another, but may also work independently or contribute different parts of a response.

questions.prompt: Which is an autonomic effector rather than a somatic skeletal-muscle effector?
questions.explanation: The ANS targets cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glands, and adipocytes.

questions.prompt: Where is the cell body of a preganglionic autonomic neuron?
options: At the skeletal motor end plate
questions.explanation: Preganglionic autonomic neurons originate in brainstem or spinal cord centers.

questions.prompt: Where is the cell body of a ganglionic autonomic neuron?
questions.explanation: Autonomic ganglia contain the neurons that send postganglionic fibers toward visceral targets.

questions.prompt: Which structure is highlighted as an integrative center for autonomic activity?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus integrates and influences autonomic regulation.

topics.title: Sympathetic origins, fibers, and ganglia
topics.cue: Thoracolumbar; short pre, long post; ganglia near the spine.

notes.text: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise in the lateral horns of spinal segments T1–L2 in this course.
Preganglionic fibers are generally short and myelinated; postganglionic fibers generally long and unmyelinated.
Paravertebral ganglia lie alongside the vertebral column and serve body-wall and other targets.
Prevertebral ganglia lie anterior to the column and serve abdominopelvic targets; celiac and mesenteric names refer to associated arteries.
White rami carry myelinated preganglionic fibers; gray rami return postganglionic fibers toward spinal nerves. Splanchnic routes reach collateral ganglia.

questions.prompt: Which spinal levels are the sympathetic preganglionic origin in this course?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic division is thoracolumbar, with preganglionic cell bodies at T1–L2.

questions.prompt: Which fiber-length pattern is typical of the sympathetic division?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic ganglia lie near the spinal cord, producing the typical short-pre/long-post arrangement.

questions.prompt: Which ganglia lie alongside the vertebral column?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic chain is the paravertebral ganglionic chain.

questions.prompt: Which rami carry myelinated sympathetic preganglionic fibers?
questions.explanation: White rami carry preganglionic fibers; gray rami contain postganglionic fibers returning toward spinal nerves.

questions.prompt: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers traveling to collateral ganglia typically pass through the chain in which way?
options: By ending in a skeletal motor end plate
By first entering the lateral ventricle
questions.explanation: The source describes preganglionic fibers passing through the chain to reach collateral ganglia through splanchnic nerves.

topics.title: Adrenal medullae and widespread activation
topics.cue: Adrenal medulla sends the signal through blood, not just one local nerve ending.

notes.text: A modified sympathetic ganglion whose secretory cells release epinephrine and norepinephrine into blood after preganglionic stimulation.
Circulating transmitters function as hormones, reaching tissues more broadly than a local postganglionic ending.
The textbook contrasts longer-lasting circulating effects with the shorter local synaptic signal.
A sympathetic preganglionic fiber can influence many ganglionic neurons, helping create coordinated widespread responses.

questions.prompt: Where does the adrenal medulla release epinephrine and norepinephrine?
options: Only into a skeletal neuromuscular cleft
questions.explanation: The medullary secretory output enters blood and can affect targets throughout the body.

questions.prompt: The adrenal medulla is described as what?
questions.explanation: Its cells receive sympathetic preganglionic input and provide a hormonal output.

questions.prompt: Which anatomical feature helps sympathetic activation affect many targets?
options: A single direct skeletal-muscle connection only
questions.explanation: Divergence allows one preganglionic fiber to influence many ganglionic neurons.

topics.title: ACh, norepinephrine, and varicosities
topics.cue: All autonomic preganglionic: ACh. Most sympathetic postganglionic: NE. Parasympathetic: ACh.

notes.text: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, exciting ganglionic neurons.
Most sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine; the textbook adds cholinergic and nitroxidergic exceptions. Parasympathetic neurons release ACh.
Swollen regions along autonomic axon branches contain transmitter vesicles and release transmitter near target cells.
The text describes NE reuptake and breakdown by MAO/COMT; ACh is rapidly inactivated by cholinesterases.
The lecture's general postganglionic-NE rule should not be read as 'every sympathetic target uses NE.'

questions.prompt: What transmitter is released by autonomic preganglionic neurons in both major divisions?
questions.explanation: Both divisions use ACh at their preganglionic-to-ganglionic synapses.

questions.prompt: Which transmitter is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons?
questions.explanation: Most sympathetic ganglionic neurons are adrenergic; the textbook explicitly notes exceptions.

questions.prompt: What is a varicosity in this context?
options: A transmitter-containing swelling along an autonomic axon branch
questions.explanation: Varicosities contain vesicles and release transmitter near visceral target cells.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme pair is associated with norepinephrine breakdown in the text?
questions.explanation: The supplied text names monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase in NE inactivation.

topics.title: Adrenergic receptors and target responses
topics.cue: Same messenger, different receptor, different response.

notes.text: The source associates activation with intracellular calcium release and often an excitatory smooth-muscle response.
The source associates activation with reduced cAMP and inhibitory effects. Its precise location wording differs between the book's prose and table, so that location is not tested here.
Associated with increased cardiac activity and metabolic effects.
Associated with relaxation of smooth muscle, including increased airway diameter.
Associated with lipolysis in adipose tissue in the textbook note.
Adrenergic receptors act through G proteins and intracellular signaling rather than being treated as one universal excitatory channel.

questions.prompt: Which adrenergic receptor is associated with increased heart rate and contraction strength in the source explanation?
questions.explanation: The textbook uses cardiac beta-1 stimulation as an example of increased activity.

questions.prompt: Which receptor is associated with relaxation of airway smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Beta-2 stimulation relaxes respiratory smooth muscle and widens the passageways in the source description.

questions.prompt: Which receptor is associated with lipolysis in adipose tissue in the textbook note?
questions.explanation: The beta-3 note identifies adipose lipolysis as its effect.

questions.prompt: Which intracellular change is paired with alpha-2 activation in the supplied table?
options: Elimination of all calcium from the body
questions.explanation: The table pairs alpha-2 receptors with reduced cAMP and inhibitory effects.

topics.title: Parasympathetic craniosacral pathways
topics.cue: Craniosacral; long pre, short post; ganglia near or within targets.

notes.text: Cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X plus spinal segments S2–S4 carry parasympathetic outflow in the course.
Long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers give localized target effects.
Terminal ganglia lie near the target organ; intramural ganglia lie in its wall.
Ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular, and otic ganglia are shown with cranial routes.
Vagus carries the major cranial output to visceral targets; pelvic nerves carry sacral output.

questions.prompt: Which description names the parasympathetic division's origin?
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic output is associated with the brainstem and sacral segments S2–S4.

questions.prompt: Which fiber-length pattern is typical of parasympathetic pathways?
options: One long skeletal motor axon only
questions.explanation: Ganglia lie near or within targets, leaving a short postganglionic distance.

questions.prompt: Where is an intramural ganglion located?
options: Within the wall of its target organ
questions.explanation: Intramural means within the organ wall; terminal ganglia lie near the target.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve provides the largest share of parasympathetic outflow in the supplied text?
questions.explanation: The text describes vagus as providing roughly three-quarters of parasympathetic output.

topics.title: Nicotinic versus muscarinic receptors
topics.cue: Nicotinic: direct channel and excitation. Muscarinic: G protein and variable response.

notes.text: Autonomic ganglia of both divisions and somatic neuromuscular junctions.
ACh produces excitation through chemically gated channels in the source description.
Parasympathetic target junctions and cholinergic sympathetic target junctions.
G-protein-mediated effects can excite or inhibit depending on target and signaling mechanism.
Nicotine and muscarine bind their namesake receptors; the receptor names do not mean the normal neurotransmitter is nicotine or muscarine.

questions.prompt: Which cholinergic receptor is found at autonomic ganglia of both divisions?
questions.explanation: Nicotinic receptors receive the preganglionic ACh signal at autonomic ganglia.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of ACh at nicotinic receptors in the course account?
questions.explanation: The supplied sources characterize nicotinic activation as excitatory.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes muscarinic responses in the supplied textbook?
options: They can be excitatory or inhibitory
They are always excitatory like every nicotinic response
They never act through G proteins
They occur only on skeletal motor end plates
questions.explanation: Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled and their effect varies with target signaling.

questions.prompt: Which is the normal neurotransmitter for both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors?
questions.explanation: Nicotine and muscarine gave the receptors their names; ACh is the normal transmitter.

topics.title: Comparing sympathetic and parasympathetic effects
topics.cue: Compare organ by organ—not everything speeds up versus everything slows down.

notes.text: Sympathetic activity mobilizes energy and increases alertness; parasympathetic activity supports food processing, nutrient uptake, and energy conservation.
Sympathetic input increases rate/force; parasympathetic input reduces them in the supplied comparison.
Sympathetic activation generally decreases digestive activity; parasympathetic activation increases motility and secretion.
Sympathetic beta-2 effects increase diameter; parasympathetic activity decreases diameter in the table.

The lecture's broad 'decreased sweating' parasympathetic summary differs from the organ table, which lists no parasympathetic innervation. This point is kept as a source note, not an unqualified quiz answer.

questions.prompt: Which response fits the general sympathetic pattern during a threatening encounter?
options: Increased heart rate and mobilization of energy reserves
Increased digestive motility as the dominant effect
Widespread production of CSF as the primary response
questions.explanation: The course describes sympathetic activation as preparing for action and mobilizing resources.

questions.prompt: Which response fits the general parasympathetic pattern after a meal?
options: Increased skeletal motor-unit recruitment as its direct output
Release of epinephrine from the adrenal medulla
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic activity supports digestion and nutrient processing.

questions.prompt: Why is 'sympathetic always excites every target' an unreliable summary of the source material?
options: Effects depend on the receptor and target tissue
Every organ receives only somatic innervation
questions.explanation: The receptor tables show both excitatory and inhibitory sympathetic effects.

questions.prompt: Which paired cardiac effect matches the course comparison?
options: Sympathetic increases rate; parasympathetic reduces rate
Both divisions must increase rate equally
Parasympathetic increases rate; sympathetic reduces rate
questions.explanation: The heart receives opposing autonomic influences in the supplied comparison.

topics.title: Dual innervation, autonomic tone, and plexuses
topics.cue: Tone gives a baseline that can rise or fall.

notes.text: Many organs receive input from both major ANS divisions, often with opposing effects; it is not a claim that every organ does.
A background level of ongoing activity permits increases or decreases in stimulation.
The supplied text describes parasympathetic influence as predominant under resting conditions.
Cardiac serves heart, pulmonary serves lungs, esophageal surrounds the esophageal route, and celiac/hypogastric networks serve abdominal/pelvic regions.
The text uses sympathetic vessel tone to illustrate graded control without requiring dual innervation.

questions.prompt: What is autonomic tone?
options: The color of an autonomic ganglion
The maximum force of skeletal muscle
questions.explanation: Autonomic tone is ongoing baseline activity that can be increased or decreased.

questions.prompt: Why does a baseline level of activity improve control?
options: Activity can be adjusted upward or downward
It prevents any response to changing conditions
It removes the need for receptors
It turns motor neurons into sensory neurons
questions.explanation: A resting baseline allows regulation in both directions rather than only activation from zero.

questions.prompt: Which plexus is associated with the lungs?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary plexus supplies autonomic fibers associated with the lungs.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes dual innervation?
options: An organ receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic input
A single neuron has exactly two dendrites
An organ receives two identical motor end plates only
Every tissue receives exactly two cranial nerves
questions.explanation: Dual innervation refers to input from both major autonomic divisions.

topics.title: Short and long visceral reflexes
topics.cue: Long loop visits CNS; short loop stays peripheral.

notes.text: Automatic response involving visceral sensory input and autonomic output; higher centers can modify it.
Sensory input reaches the CNS, processing occurs there, and preganglionic/postganglionic output reaches the target.
Local processing in peripheral autonomic/enteric circuits bypasses the CNS.
Short reflexes are particularly important for local digestive activity; the ENS can coordinate digestive functions independently of an individual CNS command.
Medullary centers coordinate visceral activity and are influenced by hypothalamic and other higher centers.

questions.prompt: Which structure does a short visceral reflex bypass?
questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature of the short reflex is that processing does not require a CNS loop.

questions.prompt: Where does processing occur in a long visceral reflex?
questions.explanation: Long visceral reflexes bring sensory input into CNS processing centers.

questions.prompt: Where are short visceral reflexes particularly important in the supplied description?
questions.explanation: Local enteric circuits provide important control of digestive functions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about visceral reflexes matches the course?
options: They require conscious decisions every time
questions.explanation: The source describes visceral reflexes as polysynaptic and subject to modulation.

topics.title: Memory categories and consolidation
topics.cue: Short-term → consolidation → long-term; repetition promotes retention.

notes.text: Fact memories concern information; skill memories concern learned motor behaviors.
Information can be recalled immediately while it persists; repetition can support conversion into longer-term storage.
Conversion of short-term memories into long-term memories. The textbook emphasizes hippocampal involvement.
In the source terminology, secondary long-term memories can fade or require effort to recall; tertiary memories persist for a lifetime.
The lecture defines a memory engram as a circuit representing a memory. The textbook treats this as a functional description, not a fully mapped anatomical blueprint.
The book discusses altered transmitter release, facilitation, and additional synaptic connections with repeated activity.

questions.prompt: What is memory consolidation?
options: Conversion of short-term memory into long-term memory
questions.explanation: Consolidation is the transition from short-term to longer-term memory storage.

questions.prompt: Which category best fits learning how to perform a practiced motor task?
questions.explanation: Skill memories are learned motor behaviors.

questions.prompt: In this textbook's terminology, which long-term memories may fade and require effort to recall?
questions.explanation: The course distinguishes secondary memories from enduring tertiary memories.

questions.prompt: Which structure is especially associated with consolidating new long-term memories?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is important to converting short-term memories into new long-term ones.

questions.prompt: What does 'memory engram' refer to in the supplied course description?
options: A neural circuit representing a memory
questions.explanation: The lecture describes an engram as a circuit corresponding to a memory.

topics.title: Sleep states and the reticular activating system
topics.cue: RAS raises alertness; REM has active dreaming with reduced body-muscle tone.

notes.text: The course describes slow-wave/NREM sleep with lower cortical activity and reduced physiological activity.
Associated with dreaming, rapid eye movements, and markedly reduced muscle tone; its EEG resembles an awake pattern in the provided figure.
REM and deep-sleep periods alternate; the lecture graph is an illustrative pattern, not an exact personal sleep schedule.
A brainstem network, with the midbrain described as its headquarters, receives sensory input and influences thalamic/cortical activity.
Stimulation of the RAS promotes wakefulness and attentiveness. Ordinary sleep can be interrupted by sensory stimuli; coma is not simply normal sleep.

questions.prompt: Which sleep state is associated with rapid eye movements and active dreaming in the source?
questions.explanation: REM is rapid eye movement sleep and is associated with active dreaming in the course.

questions.prompt: How is skeletal-muscle tone described during REM sleep?
options: Maximally increased in every skeletal muscle
Identical to a maximal voluntary contraction
questions.explanation: The text describes strong inhibition of many somatic motor neurons and reduced tone during REM, with eye movements continuing.

questions.prompt: What happens when the reticular activating system is stimulated?
questions.explanation: RAS activity promotes cortical activation, alertness, and attention.

questions.prompt: Where is the RAS located in the course description?
questions.explanation: The RAS extends through brainstem reticular formation, with the midbrain emphasized.

cards.front: Which set contains only the three brainstem regions?
cards.back: Midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata. The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.

cards.front: Which major region is most associated with conscious thought and intellectual functions in the course overview?
cards.back: Cerebrum. The overview associates the cerebrum with conscious thought, intellect, and memory.

cards.front: What is the name for an elevated fold on the cerebral surface?
cards.back: Gyrus. A gyrus is a raised fold; sulci and fissures are grooves.

cards.front: Which region helps adjust ongoing movements rather than serving as the principal site of conscious thought?
cards.back: Cerebellum. The cerebellum coordinates motor patterns and adjusts motor output.

cards.front: Which secondary vesicle develops into the cerebrum?
cards.back: Telencephalon. The development table pairs telencephalon with cerebrum and lateral ventricles.

cards.front: Which secondary vesicle produces both the pons and cerebellum?
cards.back: Metencephalon. The metencephalon is a hindbrain subdivision that forms the pons and cerebellum.

cards.front: Which adult structure develops from the myelencephalon?
cards.back: Medulla oblongata. The myelencephalon develops into the medulla oblongata.

cards.front: Which primary vesicle does not split into two secondary vesicles in the course table?
cards.back: Mesencephalon. The mesencephalon remains the midbrain; forebrain and hindbrain subdivide.

cards.front: Which passage connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle?
cards.back: Cerebral aqueduct. The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain between the third and fourth ventricles.

cards.front: Each lateral ventricle communicates with the third ventricle through which opening?
cards.back: Interventricular foramen. The interventricular foramina connect the lateral ventricles with the third ventricle.

cards.front: Which cells line the ventricles?
cards.back: Ependymal cells. Ependymal cells form the ventricular lining described in the textbook.

cards.front: Which ventricle lies in the diencephalon?
cards.back: Third ventricle. The third ventricle is the ventricular chamber of the diencephalon.

cards.front: Where is CSF produced and maintained?
cards.back: Choroid plexuses. Choroid plexuses produce CSF; venous sinuses receive returning fluid rather than producing it.

cards.front: Which structure returns CSF to the venous circulation?
cards.back: Arachnoid granulations. Arachnoid granulations project toward dural venous sinuses and allow CSF resorption.

cards.front: From the fourth ventricle, which openings lead to the subarachnoid space?
cards.back: Two lateral apertures and one median aperture. These apertures connect the fourth ventricle with the subarachnoid space.

cards.front: Which is a listed function of CSF?
cards.back: Supporting the brain through buoyancy. CSF provides buoyancy, cushioning, and a transport medium.

cards.front: What can impaired CSF resorption cause?
cards.back: Hydrocephalus. Failure of fluid removal can cause abnormal CSF accumulation.

cards.front: Which meninx closely follows the brain surface?
cards.back: Pia mater. The pia mater closely adheres to the brain surface; the arachnoid does not follow every fold.

cards.front: Which dural fold separates the cerebral hemispheres?
cards.back: Falx cerebri. The falx cerebri extends into the longitudinal cerebral fissure.

cards.front: Which fold separates the cerebrum from the cerebellum?
cards.back: Tentorium cerebelli. The tentorium cerebelli forms the partition above the cerebellum.

cards.front: CSF in the subarachnoid space lies between which layers?
cards.back: Arachnoid and pia. The subarachnoid space is between arachnoid mater and pia mater.

cards.front: Which cells form the tightly joined capillary lining central to the BBB?
cards.back: Endothelial cells. Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells are central to the BBB.

cards.front: What role do astrocytes have in the BBB according to the sources?
cards.back: They influence endothelial permeability and junctions. Astrocytes provide signals that support and regulate the endothelial barrier.

cards.front: Which cells create the blood–CSF barrier at the choroid plexus?
cards.back: Specialized ependymal cells. Specialized ependymal cells joined by tight junctions control access to CSF at the choroid plexus.

cards.front: Which is one of the areas highlighted as an exception to the usual BBB pattern?
cards.back: Pineal gland. The lecture and textbook list the pineal gland among the highlighted exceptions.

cards.front: Which region contains the respiratory rhythmicity centers described as setting the basic breathing pace?
cards.back: Medulla oblongata. The course locates the basic respiratory rhythmicity centers in the medulla.

cards.front: The cardiac and vasomotor centers are subdivisions of which group?
cards.back: Cardiovascular centers. The lecture subdivides cardiovascular control into cardiac and vasomotor centers.

cards.front: Gracile and cuneate nuclei relay somatic sensory information toward which structure?
cards.back: Thalamus. These medullary nuclei relay ascending somatic sensory information toward the thalamus.

cards.front: Which brainstem region directly connects with the spinal cord?
cards.back: Medulla oblongata. The medulla is the inferior connection between the brain and spinal cord.

cards.front: In the course naming rule, what does the first part of a tract name usually indicate?
cards.back: Its origin. The lecture teaches origin first and destination second when interpreting these tract names.

cards.front: A spinothalamic tract carries information from where to where?
cards.back: Spinal cord to thalamus. Spino- identifies spinal origin; -thalamic identifies the thalamic destination.

cards.front: Which pontine centers modify medullary respiratory activity in the course?
cards.back: Apneustic and pneumotaxic centers. These pontine centers adjust the respiratory rhythmicity centers of the medulla.

cards.front: Which cranial-nerve group is associated with the pons in the lecture?
cards.back: V, VI, VII, and VIII in part. The pons slide identifies nuclei for V, VI, VII, and VIII in part.

cards.front: A sudden bright light triggers reflexive head and eye movements. Which midbrain structures are highlighted for this role?
cards.back: Superior colliculi. The superior colliculi are associated with reflex responses to visual stimuli.

cards.front: Which midbrain structures are associated with auditory reflex processing?
cards.back: Inferior colliculi. The inferior colliculi process auditory information and reflex responses.

cards.front: Which neurotransmitter is associated with neurons of the substantia nigra in this chapter?
cards.back: Dopamine. The chapter links substantia nigra neurons with dopamine and regulation of basal-nuclei activity.

cards.front: Which nucleus is associated with subconscious upper-limb position and background muscle tone?
cards.back: Red nucleus. The red nucleus is identified with upper-limb position and muscle-tone regulation.

cards.front: The superior and inferior colliculi together are called what?
cards.back: Corpora quadrigemina. The two pairs of colliculi are collectively the corpora quadrigemina.

cards.front: What is the arbor vitae?
cards.back: Branching white matter of the cerebellum. Its tree-like appearance in section gives cerebellar white matter the name arbor vitae.

cards.front: Which cells are large, highly branched neurons of the cerebellar cortex?
cards.back: Purkinje cells. Purkinje cells are prominent processing neurons in cerebellar cortical tissue.

cards.front: Which cerebellar peduncles communicate primarily with the pons?
cards.back: Middle. Middle cerebellar peduncles carry communications with the pons.

cards.front: Which term describes the impaired coordination discussed with cerebellar damage?
cards.back: Ataxia. The lecture uses ataxia for deterioration of muscular coordination.

cards.front: Which midline cerebellar landmark is named in the source figures?
cards.back: Vermis. The vermis lies along the cerebellar midline.

cards.front: Which thalamic structure relays visual information toward the visual cortex?
cards.back: Lateral geniculate body. The lateral geniculate body is the visual relay highlighted in the thalamus figure.

cards.front: Which thalamic structure relays auditory information?
cards.back: Medial geniculate body. The medial geniculate body is associated with auditory input and output.

cards.front: Which major sensory route is the textbook's exception to the usual thalamic relay before reaching cerebral areas?
cards.back: Olfactory. The textbook singles out the olfactory tract when describing the usual ascending thalamic relay.

cards.front: Which stalk connects the hypothalamus with the pituitary gland?
cards.back: Infundibulum. The infundibulum is the hypothalamic–pituitary stalk.

cards.front: Which nucleus is paired with daily circadian rhythms in the supplied table?
cards.back: Suprachiasmatic nucleus. The hypothalamic table identifies the suprachiasmatic nucleus with daily rhythms.

cards.front: Which hypothalamic region is paired with regulation of body temperature?
cards.back: Pre-optic area. The pre-optic area coordinates thermoregulatory responses in the course description.

cards.front: Which hormone is produced by the supra-optic nucleus in the supplied table?
cards.back: Antidiuretic hormone. The table pairs the supra-optic nucleus with ADH and the paraventricular nucleus with oxytocin.

cards.front: Which system is described as a functional grouping involved in emotion, motivation, and memory?
cards.back: Limbic system. The limbic system groups connected structures by their shared functions.

cards.front: Which structure is especially important for forming new long-term memories?
cards.back: Hippocampus. The hippocampus is central to new long-term memory processing in the supplied text.

cards.front: What kind of structure is the fornix?
cards.back: A white-matter tract. The fornix is a cerebral white-matter tract connecting limbic structures.

cards.front: Which structure is associated with linking emotional states to memories?
cards.back: Amygdaloid body. The textbook associates the amygdaloid body with emotional responses and memory associations.

cards.front: The central sulcus separates which lobes?
cards.back: Frontal and parietal. The precentral frontal gyrus and postcentral parietal gyrus border the central sulcus.

cards.front: Which fibers connect cortical areas within the same hemisphere?
cards.back: Association fibers. Association fibers remain within one cerebral hemisphere.

cards.front: The corpus callosum is an example of which fiber class?
cards.back: Commissural. Commissural fibers permit communication between cerebral hemispheres.

cards.front: Which component of the lentiform nucleus is more medial?
cards.back: Globus pallidus. The textbook places globus pallidus medial to the putamen.

cards.front: Where is the primary motor cortex located?
cards.back: Precentral gyrus. The precentral gyrus is the cortical motor region identified in the source.

cards.front: Where is the primary somatosensory cortex located?
cards.back: Postcentral gyrus. The postcentral gyrus receives general somatic sensory input.

cards.front: Which area is most directly associated with speech production in the course?
cards.back: Broca's area. Broca's area coordinates patterns needed for speech production.

cards.front: Which area is most directly associated with language comprehension in the course?
cards.back: Wernicke's area. Wernicke's area is associated with language comprehension in the source description.

cards.front: Which lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
cards.back: Occipital. The primary visual cortex is mapped to the occipital lobe.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve is responsible for smell?
cards.back: Olfactory (I). The olfactory nerves carry the special sensation of smell.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle?
cards.back: Trochlear (IV). The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique; abducens supplies lateral rectus.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle?
cards.back: Abducens (VI). Abducens activates lateral rectus, associated with abduction of the eye.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve is paired with muscles of mastication?
cards.back: Trigeminal (V). The mandibular division of trigeminal carries motor fibers to muscles of mastication.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve controls facial-expression muscles and carries anterior two-thirds taste?
cards.back: Facial (VII). Facial has these motor and sensory functions; glossopharyngeal carries posterior one-third taste.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve carries hearing and equilibrium information?
cards.back: Vestibulocochlear (VIII). Its cochlear branch carries hearing and its vestibular branch carries balance information.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve controls tongue movements?
cards.back: Hypoglossal (XII). The hypoglossal nerve provides motor supply to the tongue.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve is widely distributed through thoracic and abdominal viscera?
cards.back: Vagus (X). The vagus is the widely distributed cranial nerve described in the textbook.

cards.front: Which trigeminal division carries both sensory and motor fibers?
cards.back: Mandibular (V3). V3 carries sensory fibers and the motor supply to muscles of mastication.

cards.front: Which passage does the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve use?
cards.back: Foramen rotundum. The source pairs V2 with foramen rotundum and V3 with foramen ovale.

cards.front: Which group carries cranial parasympathetic output?
cards.back: III, VII, IX, X. The source identifies III, VII, IX, and X as the cranial carriers of parasympathetic fibers.

cards.front: Which afferent/efferent pair belongs to the corneal blink reflex?
cards.back: Trigeminal input; facial output. The cranial-reflex table pairs trigeminal sensory input with facial motor output for blinking.

cards.front: What does an electroencephalogram record?
cards.back: Electrical activity of the brain. An EEG records brain electrical activity as wave patterns.

cards.front: Which wave category is associated with awake resting adults with eyes closed in the supplied text?
cards.back: Alpha. The course associates alpha with relaxed awake rest and beta with concentration.

cards.front: Which wave category is associated with intense concentration in the course figure?
cards.back: Beta. Beta is paired with concentration in the supplied figure.

cards.front: Which category is associated with deep sleep in the source figure?
cards.back: Delta. The figure pairs delta waves with deep sleep.

cards.front: What is perception in the course terminology?
cards.back: Conscious awareness of a sensation. Perception is the conscious awareness of arriving sensory information.

cards.front: A receptor responds strongly to pressure but not to the same amount of chemical stimulation. Which concept is illustrated?
cards.back: Receptor specificity. Receptor specificity describes sensitivity to particular stimulus types.

cards.front: How is a stronger sustained sensory stimulus commonly represented along its sensory axon?
cards.back: Increased action-potential frequency. The textbook describes frequency and pattern as the sensory code rather than variable action-potential height.

cards.front: Which division carries sensory input toward the CNS?
cards.back: Afferent division. Afferent pathways convey arriving sensory information.

cards.front: Which receptive field would generally provide more precise localization?
cards.back: A smaller field. A smaller field narrows the region from which the stimulus could have arisen.

cards.front: Which receptor pattern best emphasizes a change in stimulation rather than a continuing stable stimulus?
cards.back: Phasic. Phasic receptors respond particularly to changes and adapt quickly.

cards.front: Which receptor category is described as always active in the course?
cards.back: Tonic. Tonic receptors provide ongoing activity that changes with stimulation.

cards.front: Reduced transmission along a CNS sensory pathway despite continuing receptor input is which textbook category?
cards.back: Central adaptation. Central adaptation occurs within CNS processing pathways; peripheral adaptation involves the receptor's activity.

cards.front: Which receptor category monitors body position and movement?
cards.back: Proprioceptors. Proprioceptors supply information about skeletal-muscle and joint position or movement.

cards.front: Which receptor type is also called a pain receptor?
cards.back: Nociceptor. Nociceptors detect stimuli associated with potential or actual tissue damage in this course.

cards.front: Which receptor class is sensitive to physical distortion of its membrane?
cards.back: Mechanoreceptor. Mechanoreceptors respond to pressure, stretch, or related mechanical distortion.

cards.front: Which category monitors the internal environment of visceral organs?
cards.back: Interoceptors. Interoceptors monitor internal organs and their conditions.

cards.front: Which receptor is stimulated by hair movement?
cards.back: Root hair plexus. A root hair plexus consists of sensory endings associated with the hair root.

cards.front: Which skin receptors are associated with shape and texture?
cards.back: Tactile discs. Tactile discs detect fine touch and pressure and are sensitive to shape and texture.

cards.front: Which receptor detects deep pressure and high-frequency vibration?
cards.back: Lamellar (Pacinian) corpuscle. The supplied figure identifies lamellar corpuscles with deep pressure and high-frequency vibration.

cards.front: Which receptor detects fine touch and low-frequency vibration?
cards.back: Tactile (Meissner) corpuscle. Tactile corpuscles are paired with fine touch, pressure, and low-frequency vibration.

cards.front: Bulbous or Ruffini corpuscles are associated with what?
cards.back: Pressure and distortion of the deep dermis. The figure places bulbous corpuscles in the deep dermis and associates them with distortion and pressure.

cards.front: Which receptor type in the carotid sinus provides information about blood pressure?
cards.back: Baroreceptor. Baroreceptors detect stretch associated with pressure changes.
