cards.front: Which cranial nerve carries carotid-body chemoreceptor information in the lecture figure?
cards.back: Glossopharyngeal (IX). The source figure labels the carotid-body sensory route with CN IX.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve carries aortic-body chemoreceptor information in that figure?
cards.back: Vagus (X). The figure pairs aortic-body sensory input with CN X.

cards.front: Which proprioceptor is most directly associated with muscle length?
cards.back: Muscle spindle. Muscle spindles provide length-related proprioceptive input; Golgi tendon organs monitor tension.

cards.front: Which tract is associated with pain and temperature in the lecture?
cards.back: Lateral spinothalamic. The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensations.

cards.front: Which pathway carries highly localized fine touch and vibration toward conscious perception?
cards.back: Posterior column–medial lemniscus. The posterior column pathway carries fine touch, vibration, pressure, and proprioception.

cards.front: Where do second-order spinothalamic axons cross in the supplied pathway description?
cards.back: Spinal cord. They cross within the spinal cord before ascending toward the thalamus.

cards.front: The spinocerebellar pathway carries information primarily to which destination?
cards.back: Cerebellum. It provides the cerebellum with proprioceptive information for movement coordination.

cards.front: In the conscious sensory pathways shown, third-order neuron cell bodies are found in which region?
cards.back: Thalamus. Third-order thalamic neurons relay to the primary somatosensory cortex.

cards.front: Which neuron directly innervates skeletal muscle in the somatic motor pathway?
cards.back: Lower motor neuron. Lower motor neuron axons form the final somatic motor connection to skeletal muscle.

cards.front: Which tract carries commands to motor nuclei of cranial nerves?
cards.back: Corticobulbar. Corticobulbar fibers descend to brainstem cranial-nerve motor nuclei.

cards.front: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross according to the supplied table?
cards.back: Pyramids of the medulla oblongata. The lateral corticospinal fibers decussate at the medullary pyramids.

cards.front: Which descending tract arises from red nuclei?
cards.back: Rubrospinal. Rubrospinal fibers originate in the red nuclei of the midbrain.

cards.front: Which descending pathway is especially associated with balance and muscle tone?
cards.back: Vestibulospinal. Vestibulospinal tracts carry postural and balance-related motor commands.

cards.front: What does referred pain mean in this chapter?
cards.back: Pain is perceived away from its actual source. Referred pain concerns a mismatch between the origin of visceral input and its perceived location.

cards.front: Which statement preserves the lecture's caution about cardiac referred pain?
cards.back: It may be felt in the left arm, but not always. The lecture explicitly includes the qualification 'but not always'; it does not make location diagnostic.

cards.front: Which structure uses sensory feedback to fine-tune ongoing movements?
cards.back: Cerebellum. The cerebellum compares sensory information and motor activity to refine movement.

cards.front: Do the basal nuclei directly innervate skeletal muscle fibers in these pathways?
cards.back: No; they adjust motor pathway activity. The textbook describes basal-nuclei effects through upper motor pathways and feedback loops, not direct muscle innervation.

cards.front: Which is an autonomic effector rather than a somatic skeletal-muscle effector?
cards.back: Cardiac muscle. The ANS targets cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, glands, and adipocytes.

cards.front: Where is the cell body of a preganglionic autonomic neuron?
cards.back: In the CNS. Preganglionic autonomic neurons originate in brainstem or spinal cord centers.

cards.front: Where is the cell body of a ganglionic autonomic neuron?
cards.back: In a peripheral autonomic ganglion. Autonomic ganglia contain the neurons that send postganglionic fibers toward visceral targets.

cards.front: Which structure is highlighted as an integrative center for autonomic activity?
cards.back: Hypothalamus. The hypothalamus integrates and influences autonomic regulation.

cards.front: Which spinal levels are the sympathetic preganglionic origin in this course?
cards.back: T1–L2. The sympathetic division is thoracolumbar, with preganglionic cell bodies at T1–L2.

cards.front: Which fiber-length pattern is typical of the sympathetic division?
cards.back: Short preganglionic; long postganglionic. Sympathetic ganglia lie near the spinal cord, producing the typical short-pre/long-post arrangement.

cards.front: Which ganglia lie alongside the vertebral column?
cards.back: Sympathetic chain ganglia. The sympathetic chain is the paravertebral ganglionic chain.

cards.front: Which rami carry myelinated sympathetic preganglionic fibers?
cards.back: White rami communicantes. White rami carry preganglionic fibers; gray rami contain postganglionic fibers returning toward spinal nerves.

cards.front: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers traveling to collateral ganglia typically pass through the chain in which way?
cards.back: Without synapsing there. The source describes preganglionic fibers passing through the chain to reach collateral ganglia through splanchnic nerves.

cards.front: Where does the adrenal medulla release epinephrine and norepinephrine?
cards.back: Into the bloodstream. The medullary secretory output enters blood and can affect targets throughout the body.

cards.front: The adrenal medulla is described as what?
cards.back: A modified sympathetic ganglion. Its cells receive sympathetic preganglionic input and provide a hormonal output.

cards.front: Which anatomical feature helps sympathetic activation affect many targets?
cards.back: Extensive divergence of preganglionic fibers. Divergence allows one preganglionic fiber to influence many ganglionic neurons.

cards.front: What transmitter is released by autonomic preganglionic neurons in both major divisions?
cards.back: Acetylcholine. Both divisions use ACh at their preganglionic-to-ganglionic synapses.

cards.front: Which transmitter is released by most sympathetic postganglionic neurons?
cards.back: Norepinephrine. Most sympathetic ganglionic neurons are adrenergic; the textbook explicitly notes exceptions.

cards.front: What is a varicosity in this context?
cards.back: A transmitter-containing swelling along an autonomic axon branch. Varicosities contain vesicles and release transmitter near visceral target cells.

cards.front: Which enzyme pair is associated with norepinephrine breakdown in the text?
cards.back: MAO and COMT. The supplied text names monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase in NE inactivation.

cards.front: Which adrenergic receptor is associated with increased heart rate and contraction strength in the source explanation?
cards.back: Beta-1. The textbook uses cardiac beta-1 stimulation as an example of increased activity.

cards.front: Which receptor is associated with relaxation of airway smooth muscle?
cards.back: Beta-2. Beta-2 stimulation relaxes respiratory smooth muscle and widens the passageways in the source description.

cards.front: Which receptor is associated with lipolysis in adipose tissue in the textbook note?
cards.back: Beta-3. The beta-3 note identifies adipose lipolysis as its effect.

cards.front: Which intracellular change is paired with alpha-2 activation in the supplied table?
cards.back: Decreased cAMP. The table pairs alpha-2 receptors with reduced cAMP and inhibitory effects.

cards.front: Which description names the parasympathetic division's origin?
cards.back: Craniosacral. Parasympathetic output is associated with the brainstem and sacral segments S2–S4.

cards.front: Which fiber-length pattern is typical of parasympathetic pathways?
cards.back: Long preganglionic; short postganglionic. Ganglia lie near or within targets, leaving a short postganglionic distance.

cards.front: Where is an intramural ganglion located?
cards.back: Within the wall of its target organ. Intramural means within the organ wall; terminal ganglia lie near the target.

cards.front: Which cranial nerve provides the largest share of parasympathetic outflow in the supplied text?
cards.back: Vagus (X). The text describes vagus as providing roughly three-quarters of parasympathetic output.

cards.front: Which cholinergic receptor is found at autonomic ganglia of both divisions?
cards.back: Nicotinic. Nicotinic receptors receive the preganglionic ACh signal at autonomic ganglia.

cards.front: What is the effect of ACh at nicotinic receptors in the course account?
cards.back: Excitation. The supplied sources characterize nicotinic activation as excitatory.

cards.front: Which statement correctly describes muscarinic responses in the supplied textbook?
cards.back: They can be excitatory or inhibitory. Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled and their effect varies with target signaling.

cards.front: Which is the normal neurotransmitter for both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors?
cards.back: Acetylcholine. Nicotine and muscarine gave the receptors their names; ACh is the normal transmitter.

cards.front: Which response fits the general sympathetic pattern during a threatening encounter?
cards.back: Increased heart rate and mobilization of energy reserves. The course describes sympathetic activation as preparing for action and mobilizing resources.

cards.front: Which response fits the general parasympathetic pattern after a meal?
cards.back: Increased digestive motility and secretion. Parasympathetic activity supports digestion and nutrient processing.

cards.front: Why is 'sympathetic always excites every target' an unreliable summary of the source material?
cards.back: Effects depend on the receptor and target tissue. The receptor tables show both excitatory and inhibitory sympathetic effects.

cards.front: Which paired cardiac effect matches the course comparison?
cards.back: Sympathetic increases rate; parasympathetic reduces rate. The heart receives opposing autonomic influences in the supplied comparison.

cards.front: What is autonomic tone?
cards.back: Background autonomic neural activity. Autonomic tone is ongoing baseline activity that can be increased or decreased.

cards.front: Why does a baseline level of activity improve control?
cards.back: Activity can be adjusted upward or downward. A resting baseline allows regulation in both directions rather than only activation from zero.

cards.front: Which plexus is associated with the lungs?
cards.back: Pulmonary plexus. The pulmonary plexus supplies autonomic fibers associated with the lungs.

cards.front: Which statement describes dual innervation?
cards.back: An organ receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic input. Dual innervation refers to input from both major autonomic divisions.

cards.front: Which structure does a short visceral reflex bypass?
cards.back: CNS. The distinguishing feature of the short reflex is that processing does not require a CNS loop.

cards.front: Where does processing occur in a long visceral reflex?
cards.back: CNS. Long visceral reflexes bring sensory input into CNS processing centers.

cards.front: Where are short visceral reflexes particularly important in the supplied description?
cards.back: Digestive tract and associated glands. Local enteric circuits provide important control of digestive functions.

cards.front: Which statement about visceral reflexes matches the course?
cards.back: They are polysynaptic. The source describes visceral reflexes as polysynaptic and subject to modulation.

cards.front: What is memory consolidation?
cards.back: Conversion of short-term memory into long-term memory. Consolidation is the transition from short-term to longer-term memory storage.

cards.front: Which category best fits learning how to perform a practiced motor task?
cards.back: Skill memory. Skill memories are learned motor behaviors.

cards.front: In this textbook's terminology, which long-term memories may fade and require effort to recall?
cards.back: Secondary memories. The course distinguishes secondary memories from enduring tertiary memories.

cards.front: Which structure is especially associated with consolidating new long-term memories?
cards.back: Hippocampus. The hippocampus is important to converting short-term memories into new long-term ones.

cards.front: What does 'memory engram' refer to in the supplied course description?
cards.back: A neural circuit representing a memory. The lecture describes an engram as a circuit corresponding to a memory.

cards.front: Which sleep state is associated with rapid eye movements and active dreaming in the source?
cards.back: REM sleep. REM is rapid eye movement sleep and is associated with active dreaming in the course.

cards.front: How is skeletal-muscle tone described during REM sleep?
cards.back: Markedly reduced. The text describes strong inhibition of many somatic motor neurons and reduced tone during REM, with eye movements continuing.

cards.front: What happens when the reticular activating system is stimulated?
cards.back: Cortical activation and increased arousal. RAS activity promotes cortical activation, alertness, and attention.

cards.front: Where is the RAS located in the course description?
cards.back: Brainstem, with midbrain headquarters. The RAS extends through brainstem reticular formation, with the midbrain emphasized.

cautions.text: This version uses five uploaded lecture PDFs and the 100-page textbook excerpt. No Chapter 14–16 recording or transcript has been added, and no oral lecture emphasis is inferred.

cautions.title: Fast pain versus slow pain: explicitly excluded
cautions.text: Chapter 15 lecture PDF page 3 (slide 7) says the distinction will not be asked for exam purposes. This question bank does not test that difference.

cautions.title: Final nervous-system integration figure: supplementary
cautions.text: Chapter 16 second file, PDF page 6 (slide 18), is described by the instructor as included for fun. It is kept in the source viewer but is not treated as an explicit exam priority.

cautions.title: CSF composition: wording differs between sources
cautions.text: Lecture 14 part 1, PDF page 5 uses a plasma-minus-clotting-factors shorthand. The textbook, printed page 471, instead describes selective production with differences in protein, ions, and other constituents. Both source descriptions are retained here; the shorthand is not used as an unqualified quiz answer.

cautions.title: Intracranial-pressure numbers need clarification
cautions.text: Lecture 14 part 1, PDF page 10 gives 12–21 without an unambiguous unit and then a pressure-above-normal statement. No numeric pressure question is included until the intended units and context are clarified.

cautions.title: Autonomic summaries have exceptions
cautions.text: The lecture generally pairs sympathetic postganglionic signaling with norepinephrine. The textbook also describes ACh and NO exceptions. Its organ table lists no parasympathetic sweat-gland innervation, whereas the lecture summary mentions decreased eccrine activity. This discrepancy is visible rather than silently combined into one rule.

cautions.title: Alpha-2 locations differ within the textbook
cautions.text: The prose on printed page 544 and the receptor table on page 547 give differing location descriptions. Practice tests the shared inhibition/reduced-cAMP association, not a single definitive location claim.

cautions.title: Pupillary light-reflex table discrepancy
cautions.text: Table 14–5 on printed page 507 describes light-associated constriction. Table 16–4 on page 553 has a sympathetic row describing light-associated dilation, while the surrounding discussion distinguishes light from darkness. This disputed table row is not tested in the initial bank.

cautions.title: No exam-sheet permission assumed
